sealed.statement: Establish the single owner of user-plane admission AND wire it at the statement-execution entry: before TRAFFIC_READY, control-plane capability is admitted and ordinary user work is refused with a typed retryable answer carrying the existing lifecycle progress contract, decided in one place rather than inferred from table identity. A composition with no lifecycle authority admits, typed and explicitly, because there is no formation to wait for. Replacing the routing layer's systemTable fail-open with this owner remains a later slice.

constraints.statement: If this Quest changes source code, spawn a subagent verifier before audit and git handoff, then record a Solver finding with evidence subagent:<id>.

One owner decides user-plane admission. The lifecycle predicate is the exported isTrafficReadySnapshot and the refusal is the exported buildLifecycleReadinessNotReadyError; neither is re-derived here, so no second readiness authority is created. Table identity classifies WHICH capability a statement is, at the boundary; it never decides whether the user plane is open.

No lifecycle authority present (an embedded engine with no cluster to form) admits; an authority present but yielding no readable snapshot REFUSES user work. These are distinct typed outcomes, because collapsing them would let a wiring regression read as "no cluster" and silently admit everything.
Control-plane capability is admitted before TRAFFIC_READY whether readiness is not-yet-ready or unreadable, because refusing the work that produces readiness would deadlock formation.
A refusal carries the readiness owner’s own retryAfterMs, progress contract, wake source and blocking dependency; this Quest invents no retry budget and no new error taxonomy.

The composition resolver must read a key the real seed and joiner runtime owners actually expose, and the provider must be lazy because readiness is wired after the engine is built. A gate that runs but can never refuse is not a gate; this is pinned by a receipt because it is invisible to a passing suite.

The admission owner mints no lifecycle phase, publishes nothing, and derives nothing from nodes.status, publication counts, or coverage; its decision is frozen and carries exactly admitted, reasonCode and lifecycleReadiness.
Proof is a deterministic node:test witness, with existing-readiness-predicates-unchanged as the control that must stay green; every guard is mutation-verified and no cloud run is part of the proof.

hypothesis: Add the user-plane admission owner and wire it at the statement-execution entry: before TRAFFIC_READY ordinary user work is refused with the readiness owner's own typed retryable answer, control-plane capability is admitted so formation is not deadlocked, an authority present but unreadable fails closed, and a composition with no lifecycle authority admits typed. Also fixes a latent defect in buildLifecycleReadinessNotReadyError, which mutated its input snapshot and threw on any frozen one.

evidence: verifier review-9f9e86858a6ec6097ec759c3: deleting the single wiring line left all 13 owner-level receipts green, so the slice could do nothing while fully passing

verifier review-fc52aec967e34c64cd3b4fa3: COMMIT/ROLLBACK refused (stranding open transactions), TRAFFIC_READY measured never reached with no driver in src so the gate would refuse forever, and the subquery recursion survived undisclosed

problems: system theory required after repeated same-frontier stalls

problem: This frontier has stalled twice, and both stalls were the same shape: the slice was verified against a model of the system rather than the system. Round 1 classified statements with synthetic ASTs the parser never emits (so every SELECT and every DDL statement was admitted, ungating the entire read path), pinned the provider with a source regex that matched a getter returning undefined (so the gate was permanently inert on every joining node), and consulted readiness through a projection that ADVANCED the state machine (so user traffic demoted the node it was asking about). Round 2 introduced a fail-closed rule that refused COMMIT and ROLLBACK — stranding open transactions mid-unwind — and left the gate refusing forever, because nothing in src drives lifecycle evaluation on a cadence so a production controller sits at INIT/ready:false indefinitely.
successCondition: Every scenario is driven by the real producer: statements parsed by SQLParser, the joiner owner built by createNodeJoiningRuntimeDependencyOwner, readiness taken from a real BootstrapReadinessState, and refusals observed through the real executeQuery. Seventeen receipts, and the mutations that previously survived — deleting the wiring line, ignoring ast.from, reverting the joiner getter, restoring the evaluate fallback, holding transaction control, treating an un-driven lifecycle as not-ready, dropping the subquery recursion — each now red exactly the scenario that owns them.
mechanism: Every defect came from asserting against a fixture I authored instead of the producer that actually feeds the code: hand-written ASTs instead of SQLParser output; a readFileSync regex instead of the constructed owner; a snapshot literal instead of a real LifecycleController; and a statement vocabulary reasoned about rather than parsed. Each fixture encoded what I believed the shape to be, so the receipt could only ever confirm my belief. The green suite was not evidence about the system; it was evidence about my model of it.
decidingOwner: The quest author. The tooling supplied the producers all along — SQLParser, createNodeJoiningRuntimeDependencyOwner, BootstrapReadinessState — and using them is what turned every one of these from invisible to red.
missingTransitionOrObservation: Nothing requires a witness to source its fixtures from the real producer, and nothing detects that an asserted shape has no producer at all. Both defects were invisible to a fully green suite and to every ratchet, and were found only by an independent verifier who parsed real statements and constructed the real owner.
discriminator: Build the fixture from the producer, not from belief. If a receipt asserts on a shape no component in the system emits, it measures the author, not the code. Where a producer exists — a parser, a factory, a controller — the witness must call it.

mechanism: Round 2 found three defects the receipts could not see, all from fixtures authored rather than produced. Transaction control: the fail-closed rule refused COMMIT and ROLLBACK, so application-database.js and the migration coordinator strand an open engine transaction with the record stuck in ROLLING_BACK — a node ready at BEGIN that demotes before COMMIT can neither finish nor unwind. Un-driven lifecycle: measured on the real controller, every setDependency path is reachable only through external probe entry points and nothing in src drives evaluation on a cadence, so a production controller sits at INIT/ready:false and the gate would refuse EVERY query forever. Derived tables: the parser emits {name:null, subquery} and the classifier did not recurse, so the subquery walk was removable with the bar green.
intervention: Exempt transaction-control statement types from the hold, because they are the release path rather than new work. Expose lastEvaluatedAt on the lifecycle snapshot and admit typed when it is null, so the absence of a decision is not read as a decision to hold. Recurse into derived-table subqueries. Assert each against the real producer: statements from SQLParser, readiness from a real BootstrapReadinessState.
expectedMovement: Holding transaction control, treating an un-driven lifecycle as not-ready, and dropping the subquery recursion each move from 17 pass / 0 fail to 16 pass / 1 fail; widening the un-driven branch to always-true reds seven.
negativeResultMeans: If the un-driven admit also fires for a DRIVEN not-ready controller, the gate is inert rather than safe — which is why the same scenario asserts the refusal returns once evaluate() has run.
discriminator: Distinguish the absence of a decision from a decision. A controller nobody has evaluated is not evidence that the node is unready, and a gate that cannot tell them apart either refuses forever or admits forever depending on which way it guesses.
